This video is only two weeks old and yet it is completely wrong about the miracle in Mississippi education driven by a return to basics and exclusion of all DEI baloney in our classrooms.  Get your facts straight when presenting Science-based media:

"Mississippi achieved its highest-ever national K-12 education ranking at 16th in the nation in the 2025 KIDS COUNT Data Book, a dramatic rise from 48th in 2014.

Key Literacy and Test Score Gains

• Reading & Math Rankings: Often called the "Mississippi Miracle," the state moved from 49th in 4th-grade reading on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) in 2013 to 9th in the nation by 2024, leading the nation in long-term score improvements for both reading and math.
• Economically Disadvantaged Students: Low-income 4th graders in Mississippi achieved the highest reading scores in the entire country.
• Third-Grade Promotion: Under the Literacy-Based Promotion Act, a record-high 77.3% of third-graders passed the state reading assessment on their first attempt.

Graduation Rates and Accountability

• High School Graduation: The state’s high school graduation rate rose from 75% a decade ago to 90.8% for the 2024–25 school year, surpassing the national average.
• Accountability Grades: Over 50% of Mississippi schools and districts earned a B or higher under more stringent performance cut scores implemented for the 2025–26 school year.
• District Improvements: For instance, Jackson Public Schools increased its district score by 37 points, with 20 schools now rated C or higher.

Core Drivers of Success

• Literacy Policies: Strict early-reading interventions, teacher professional development in the science of reading, and third-grade retention safeguards.
• Pre-K Standards: Mississippi remains one of just five states whose publicly funded pre-K programs meet all 10 quality standards set by the National Institute for Early Education Research (NIEER).

replies.author: @MightyBenaiah
replies.text:
When Mississippi seceded from the Union in January 1861, both of its sitting U.S. Senators—Albert G. Brown and Jefferson Davis, left their seats vacant to join the Confederacy. For nearly a decade during the war and the start of Reconstruction, those Class 1 and Class 2 Senate seats remained empty.
When Mississippi was finally readmitted to the Union in 1870, the newly integrated state legislature had to fill the remaining unexpired terms for both vacant seats at the same time.
The Mississippi legislature agreed to elect a Black candidate to finish out the shorter remaining term (ending in March 1871) and a white candidate for the longer remaining term (ending in 1875).
The legislature officially voted to place Hiram Revels in Albert G. Brown’s former seat. They chose a white Union general, Adelbert Ames, to fill Jefferson Davis’s former seat.
